title: The near neighbor and the far
hookLine: kindness to parents, kin, orphans, the needy, neighbors near and far, travelers (4:36)

cards: Quick test. How many of your neighbors do you know by name? The people on either side, across the hall, across the street?
Many people in big cities would answer one, maybe two. A podcast host's opinions can be better known than the name of the person whose kitchen shares your wall.
An-Nisa has a verse that lists the people you owe kindness to, in widening circles, and neighbors appear on it twice.

teach.b: Verse 36 begins: worship God and associate nothing with Him. Then it moves straight to people, as if the two belong together. Be good to parents, relatives, orphans, the needy.

teach.h: THE NEAR NEIGHBOR AND THE FAR
teach.b: To the neighbor who is near, and the neighbor who is far.
To the companion at your side, the traveler, and those in your care. And it ends: God does not love the proud and the boastful. Al-jar dhi al-qurba, the near neighbor.
Al-jar al-junub, the distant one, the stranger neighbor. Commentators read the pair in a few ways: a relative nearby and a neighbor who isn't related, or near in distance and farther down the road.
Some early scholars said the far neighbor includes a neighbor of another faith. All the readings agree on one thing: being a neighbor creates a duty, whoever they are.
The companion at your side, as-sahib bil-janb, is read as a fellow traveler, a coworker, a spouse: whoever happens to be next to you. The hadith collections press the point hard.

teach.h: AS IF THE NEIGHBOR WOULD INHERIT
teach.b: In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet ﷺ said the angel Jibril kept urging him to be good to the neighbor until he thought the neighbor would be made an heir. In another report, he said three times: by God, he does not believe.

teach.h: THE NEIGHBOR WHO IS NOT OF KIN.
teach.b: Asked who, he answered: the one whose neighbor is not safe from his harm. So the far neighbor isn't optional. The verse lists them right next to your parents.

how: Muslims treat kindness to neighbors as a religious duty, whatever the neighbor's faith; many share food with neighbors at Eid and in Ramadan, following 4:36 and the hadith about Jibril's repeated urging.

o: the companion who sits at your side
the far neighbor, the stranger next door
a traveler passing through on the road

games.q: the near neighbor and the far — tap the pairs.
p: kept urging kindness to the neighbor

s: twice: the near neighbor and the far.
some early scholars included neighbors of other faiths
the far neighbor was read by some as a neighbor of another religion.
the verse ends by praising the self-made and confident
it ends: God does not love the proud and boastful.

games.q: the Prophet says three times: by God, he does not believe. his companions ask who. what does he answer?
o: the one who skips the night prayer.
the one whose neighbor is not safe from his harm.
the one who doesn't give charity.
games.why: the one whose neighbor is not safe from his harm, as Sahih al-Bukhari reports.

practice: Walk around where you live in your mind: the door to your left, your right, across the hall or the street. For each one, ask: do I know their name?
Notice the gaps without guilt, and let one neighbor you've never really met come to mind, with a simple greeting you could offer: a hello in the hallway, a wave, a plate of something on a holiday.

wordCard.voice: Al-jar al-junub, the distant neighbor, the stranger. On the list of kindness in 4:36, next to parents and kin.

orig.note: Arabic: the neighbor who is distant, a stranger (4:36).

carryVoice: Your line: the far neighbor too. Being a neighbor is enough to be owed kindness. That's day three hundred eighty-one.
